course.title: Data Science & Predictive Analytics
course.description: Progress from solid statistics and Python/SQL foundations to visualisation and introductory machine learning. Designed for learners who already have basic data literacy and want professional analytical skills.

modules.title: Module 1: Statistics for analysis
modules.description: Averages, spread, probability, correlation and sampling.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: Averages, spread and distributions
lessons.description: Mean, median, variance and shape of data.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Calculate and interpret mean, median, standard deviation and recognise basic distribution shapes.

Key ideas

Central tendency (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, variance, standard deviation) together describe a dataset. Distributions can be symmetric, skewed or multi-modal; the shape guides which statistics and visuals are appropriate.

Practice

For a small real dataset compute mean, median and a measure of spread. Sketch the shape and comment on skewness.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Probability, correlation and sampling
lessons.description: Chance, relationships and how samples represent populations.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Explain basic probability, interpret a correlation coefficient, and describe simple random sampling.

Key ideas

Probability quantifies uncertainty. Correlation measures linear association (not causation). A well-designed sample allows inference about a larger population; biased samples produce misleading results.

Practice

Find one claimed relationship in a news story and discuss whether correlation or causation is being implied.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Interpreting statistical results
lessons.description: Read results critically and avoid common mistakes.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Interpret statistical output with appropriate caution and spot common misuses.

Key ideas

Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance. Multiple testing, selection bias and poor visualisation can mislead. Always ask about sample size, data quality and alternative explanations.

lessons.title: Module 1 review and assessment
lessons.description: Module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 1 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %. Review the lessons if you need to retake.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The median is preferred over the mean when:
Data are perfectly symmetric
*Extreme values would distort the mean
Sample size is one
Data are only categories
explain: Median is robust to outliers.
level: 1

Q: Correlation measures:
Causation always
*Strength of linear association
Only the mean
Sample size
explain: Correlation ≠ causation.
level: 1

Q: A biased sample tends to:
Represent the population well
*Produce systematically misleading estimates
Increase the median automatically
Eliminate the need for charts
explain: Bias undermines inference.
level: 2

Q: Standard deviation measures:
The middle value
*Typical spread around the mean
Only the maximum
The mode
explain: SD quantifies dispersion.
level: 1

Q: Statistical significance means:
The result is important in real life
*The observed result is unlikely under a stated null model (given assumptions)
The sample is biased
The chart is colourful
explain: Significance is about evidence against a null, not automatic importance.
level: 2

Q: Skewed data often make the mean:
Identical to the median
*Pulled toward the long tail
Undefined
Equal to the range
explain: Skew pulls the mean.
level: 2

Q: A good sample should:
Only include convenient people
*Be selected so that it fairly represents the population of interest
Be as small as possible always
Ignore response rates
explain: Representativeness is key.
level: 1

Q: “Correlation implies causation” is:
Always true
*A common error
Required by statistics
Only true for large samples
explain: Causation needs stronger design/evidence.
level: 1

Q: Practical importance of a result depends on:
Only the p-value
*Context, effect size and consequences of decisions
Only the sample mean
Chart colours
explain: Context and size of effect matter.
level: 2

Q: Variance is:
The square of the standard deviation (population definition)
*A measure of spread; SD is its square root
The same as the median
Only used for categories
explain: Variance and SD are linked spread measures.
level: 2

modules.title: Module 2: Python for data
modules.description: Core Python and data handling with pandas.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Python fundamentals
lessons.description: Variables, types, control flow and functions.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Write and run simple Python scripts that use variables, lists, loops and functions.

Key ideas

Python is readable and widely used for data work. Master the basics of assignment, data types, if/else, for loops and defining small functions before moving to libraries.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Working with data in Python
lessons.description: Load tables and inspect them with pandas.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Load a CSV into a pandas DataFrame, inspect shape, columns and basic summaries.

Key ideas

pandas provides DataFrame objects that feel like super-powered spreadsheets. Start with read_csv, head, info, describe and value_counts.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Cleaning and exploring datasets
lessons.description: Handle missing values, filter rows and create simple derived columns.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Clean common data problems and compute basic group summaries in pandas.

Key ideas

Missing values, wrong types and inconsistent categories are routine. Learn dropna/fillna, astype, query/filter and groupby + agg.

lessons.title: Module 2 review and assessment
lessons.description: Module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 2 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %. Review the lessons if you need to retake.
lessons.quiz:
Q: A pandas DataFrame is best described as:
A single number
*A table of data with labelled columns and rows
Only a chart
A password
explain: DataFrames are tabular.
level: 1

Q: read_csv is used to:
Train a neural network
*Load a comma-separated file into a DataFrame
Delete columns
Plot maps
explain: read_csv imports tabular text data.
level: 1

Q: groupby in pandas is typically followed by:
Only print
*An aggregation such as mean, sum or count
Deleting the index forever
Converting to a string only
explain: Group-then-aggregate is the classic pattern.
level: 2

Q: Handling missing values may involve:
Ignoring the problem always
*Dropping rows/columns or filling with a reasoned value
Multiplying by zero
Only changing chart colours
explain: Explicit strategies are required.
level: 1

Q: A Python function is useful because:
It slows the computer
*It packages reusable logic under a clear name
It replaces all variables
It is required for every line
explain: Functions organise and reuse code.
level: 1

Q: value_counts is helpful for:
Fitting deep learning models
*Seeing frequency of categories in a column
Only numerical correlation
Deleting duplicates only
explain: value_counts summarises categorical frequency.
level: 2

Q: Before heavy cleaning you should:
Overwrite the only raw file
*Keep a copy of the original data
Share all personal data publicly
Skip inspection
explain: Preserve the source.
level: 1

Q: Filtering rows in pandas can be done with:
Only Excel macros
*Boolean conditions or query
Only SQL forever
Deleting the Python installation
explain: Boolean masks and query are standard.
level: 2

Q: describe() on a DataFrame typically shows:
Only column names
*Summary statistics for numeric columns
The full raw file
Network latency
explain: describe gives count/mean/std/quartiles etc.
level: 1

Q: Consistent data types in columns help because:
They make files larger always
*Many operations and models expect uniform types
They eliminate all missing values
They replace documentation
explain: Type consistency enables reliable computation.
level: 2

modules.title: Module 3: SQL and databases
modules.description: Query, filter, join and summarise data in tables.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Querying data with SQL
lessons.description: SELECT, FROM, WHERE and ORDER BY.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Write SELECT queries that retrieve and filter rows from a single table.

Key ideas

SQL is the standard language for relational databases. Start with SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: Filtering, joining and summarising
lessons.description: JOIN, GROUP BY and aggregate functions.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Combine tables with JOIN and produce summaries with GROUP BY and aggregates.

Key ideas

Most useful data lives in multiple related tables. INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN are the workhorses. GROUP BY + COUNT/SUM/AVG answers many business questions.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.3: Working with real tables
lessons.description: Practical patterns and common pitfalls.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Apply SQL patterns to realistic schemas and avoid common mistakes (wrong join type, missing GROUP BY columns, accidental Cartesian products).

lessons.title: Module 3 review and assessment
lessons.description: Module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 3 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %. Review the lessons if you need to retake.
lessons.quiz:
Q: SELECT is used to:
Delete a database
*Retrieve columns from tables
Create a user only
Shutdown the server
explain: SELECT reads data.
level: 1

Q: WHERE filters:
Columns after aggregation only
*Rows before grouping (in the basic pattern)
Only table names
Chart colours
explain: WHERE restricts which rows enter the result.
level: 1

Q: GROUP BY is typically used with:
Only SELECT *
*Aggregate functions such as COUNT or SUM
DROP TABLE
Password changes
explain: Grouping + aggregation produces summaries.
level: 1

Q: An INNER JOIN returns:
All rows from both tables regardless of match
*Only rows that match on the join condition
Only the first table
No rows ever
explain: Inner join keeps matches.
level: 2

Q: A LEFT JOIN keeps:
Only right-table matches
*All left-table rows and matching right-table data (or nulls)
Only aggregated totals
Nothing
explain: Left join preserves the left table.
level: 2

Q: Forgetting a non-aggregated column in GROUP BY usually:
Is always fine
*Causes an error or unpredictable results depending on the engine
Increases speed only
Deletes data
explain: GROUP BY rules must be respected.
level: 2

Q: ORDER BY controls:
Which database you connect to
*The sequence of rows in the result
User permissions
Backup frequency
explain: ORDER BY sorts the output.
level: 1

Q: COUNT(*) counts:
Only distinct values always
*The number of rows in the group (or result)
Only nulls
Only numeric columns
explain: COUNT(*) tallies rows.
level: 1

Q: A Cartesian product often results from:
A correct INNER JOIN
*A join missing its ON condition (or a cross join)
Using WHERE
Selecting fewer columns
explain: Missing join conditions multiply rows.
level: 2

Q: SQL is especially valuable because:
It only works offline
*Most organisational data sits in relational databases
It replaces all spreadsheets forever
It cannot filter rows
explain: Databases are central to real data work.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 4: Visualisation and reporting
modules.description: Design clear visuals and tell a decision-ready story.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.1: Principles of clear visuals
lessons.description: Choose the right chart and avoid misleading designs.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Select chart types that match the data and the question, and avoid common distortions.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.2: Power BI dashboards
lessons.description: Build interactive views for non-technical stakeholders.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Create a simple interactive dashboard that answers a business question in under a minute of viewing.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.3: Telling a story with data
lessons.description: Structure findings for decision makers.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Write a short narrative that links question → evidence → recommendation → next check.

lessons.title: Module 4 review and assessment
lessons.description: Module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 4 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %. Review the lessons if you need to retake.
lessons.quiz:
Q: A line chart is usually best for:
Unrelated categories
*Change over time
Parts of a whole only
Passwords
explain: Lines emphasise trends.
level: 1

Q: Truncating the y-axis can:
Never affect interpretation
*Exaggerate differences
Improve data quality
Replace titles
explain: Scale choices influence perception.
level: 2

Q: A good dashboard prioritises:
Every possible chart
*The main question and the most important metrics
Only raw tables
Hidden filters only
explain: Focus serves decision makers.
level: 1

Q: Annotations on charts help:
Hide the data
*Explain peaks, changes or caveats
Increase file size only
Replace the need for data
explain: Context reduces misreading.
level: 2

Q: Pie charts become poor when:
There are two slices
*There are many small categories
Data are time series without aggregation
Both many categories and unsuitable data can be problems
explain: Too many slices hurt readability.
level: 2

Q: A decision-ready data story should include:
Only the chart
*Question, key finding, limitation, recommendation
Every SQL query
Personal attacks
explain: Transparent structure builds trust.
level: 1

Q: Interactive filters in Power BI allow:
Deleting the dataset permanently
*Users to explore segments without new reports each time
Only printing
Hiding all numbers
explain: Interactivity supports self-service exploration.
level: 2

Q: Colour should be used:
Randomly for decoration
*With purpose (categories, emphasis, accessibility)
Only in black and white always
To encode more than five independent variables at once without legend
explain: Purposeful colour aids understanding.
level: 2

Q: The source and date of data on a dashboard:
Should be hidden
*Should be visible
Are optional always
Replace the need for titles
explain: Provenance supports trust.
level: 1

Q: The main goal of a business visualisation is:
Artistic expression only
*Faster, clearer understanding that supports action
Maximum number of chart types
Hiding uncertainty always
explain: Clarity for decisions is the point.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 5: Predictive analytics and machine learning
modules.description: Introductory prediction, model testing and responsible use.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.1: Prediction and forecasting basics
lessons.description: What prediction can and cannot do.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Explain the difference between describing the past and predicting the future, and list conditions that make prediction more reliable.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.2: Machine learning models
lessons.description: Supervised learning intuition and common model families.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Describe supervised learning at a high level and name common model types (regression, tree-based, etc.).

lessons.title: Lesson 5.3: Testing and improving a model
lessons.description: Train/test splits, simple metrics and overfitting awareness.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Evaluate a model on held-out data and recognise basic signs of overfitting.

lessons.title: Module 5 review and assessment
lessons.description: Module check. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 5 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %. Review the lessons if you need to retake.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Predictive analytics mainly answers:
What happened?
*What is likely to happen?
What is the password?
Who to fire randomly
explain: Prediction looks forward.
level: 1

Q: A train/test split helps:
Use all data for training only
*Estimate how the model will perform on new data
Delete half the data permanently
Avoid all metrics
explain: Held-out data tests generalisation.
level: 1

Q: Overfitting means:
The model is too simple
*The model fits training data very well but performs poorly on new data
The model has no features
The data has no rows
explain: Overfit models memorise rather than generalise.
level: 2

Q: Supervised learning uses:
Only unlabelled data
*Input features paired with known target values
Only images
No evaluation
explain: Labels supervise the learning.
level: 1

Q: A simple useful metric for classification is:
Only the mean of features
*Accuracy, precision, recall or similar (chosen for the problem)
File size
Chart colour
explain: Metrics quantify performance.
level: 2

Q: More complex models are:
Always better
*Not automatically better; they can overfit and be harder to explain
Never useful
Required by law
explain: Complexity has costs.
level: 2

Q: Prediction quality depends heavily on:
Only the programming language
*Data quality, relevance of features and stability of the process being modelled
Only the number of charts
Random fonts
explain: Garbage in, garbage out still applies.
level: 1

Q: Using a model in production requires:
Never monitoring it again
*Ongoing monitoring because data and processes drift
Deleting all training data immediately
Hiding all errors
explain: Real-world data changes.
level: 2

Q: Ethical use of predictive models includes:
Ignoring fairness and privacy
*Considering impact on people, bias and transparency where appropriate
Maximising complexity only
Avoiding all documentation
explain: Responsibility matters.
level: 2

Q: The best first predictive project is often:
The most complex deep model possible
*A clear business question with measurable outcomes and clean enough data
A project with no data
A project that cannot be evaluated
explain: Clarity and evaluability beat complexity.
level: 1
